cf.title: BUG #19798: "failed to build any 4-way joins" with ROLLUP over a LATERAL subquery that references the nullable s

input.subject: BUG #19798: "failed to build any 4-way joins" with ROLLUP over a LATERAL subquery that references the nullable s

verdict_reasoning: The bug is real, reproducible and well analysed, and a fix is wanted. The one surviving objection, maintenance-fit-1, is a fixable design point: the patch adds a second rule in join_search_one_level() next to has_join_restriction(), and message #2 does not say whether the three join.sql plan changes of the alternative are worse. A committer who knows the join search code has to choose between the two fixes.

brief.title: Fix "failed to build any N-way joins" with grouping sets over LATERAL subquery
brief.problem: A query with grouping sets fails at plan time with "failed to build any 4-way joins" when a LATERAL subquery over two or more tables returns a column from the nullable side of an earlier outer join. The reporter bisected it to commit 90947674fc9 (2018) and reproduced it on 14 through master. The same query without grouping sets plans fine.
brief.proposed_design: With grouping sets, the pulled-up lateral output becomes a PlaceHolderVar evaluated at {c,d} that needs values from the completed b/a outer join, so the only legal final join is the bushy pair {b,a} + {c,d}. The bushy-join loop in join_search_one_level() skips {b,a} as old_rel because it has no join clauses and has_join_restriction() is false. The patch adds a local exception there for a joinrel that supplies all of a PHV's ph_lateral rels while the PHV's ph_eval_at rels are not yet joined, and leaves the pair decision to have_join_order_restriction().
author_claims: The fix is limited to bushy-join pruning in joinrels.c and keeps the existing pruning heuristic.
Standard regression tests pass with no plan changes.
Removing the preliminary check also fixes the bug but makes the planner examine more bushy-join pairs.
Changing has_join_restriction() also fixes the bug but changes three plans in join.sql and affects other parts of join search.
brief.thread_state: Only the reporter and the patch author have posted, and nobody has reviewed the patch yet. The author asks for thoughts on the chosen approach.
unclear: The patch prose does not say whether it adds a regression test for the reported queries.
The thread does not say which branches the fix should be back-patched to, though the bug reaches 14.
The author does not measure the planning-time cost of the new check on queries with many relations or many PlaceHolderVars.
The thread does not say whether the exception covers the 5-way and 6-way variants, nor whether the author tested them.
The thread does not say whether the joinrel's lateral_referencers being always NULL should be fixed instead.

objections.title: Local pruning exception duplicates the meaning of has_join_restriction()
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how PlaceHolderVars or lateral references restrict join order and updates has_join_restriction() only. The bushy-loop exception keeps the old rule. A new "failed to build any N-way joins" error then appears on some grouping-sets or lateral query, found later by a fuzzer or a user.
objections.argument: After this patch, the join search has two places that decide whether a rel takes part in a join-order restriction: has_join_restriction() and the new exception in join_search_one_level(). Nothing fails if they drift apart. Message #2 rejects fixing has_join_restriction() because three join.sql plans change, but it does not say whether those plans get worse. A committer would likely prefer one definition of "has a join restriction", or a fix to the joinrel lateral_referencers that message #1 says is always NULL.
objections.author_must_show: Are the three join.sql plan changes from the has_join_restriction() fix actually worse, and if not, why keep a second, local rule?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 explains the choice by three join.sql plan changes and wider effects, but does not say whether those plans are worse. The patch adds a second rule that must track has_join_restriction() and have_join_order_restriction(), and nothing fails if they drift.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The patch changes which bushy-join pairs join_search_one_level() considers in joinrels.c.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The bug reproduces on 14 through master, and the thread does not name the target branches.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The new exception is a second join-restriction rule that must stay in step with has_join_restriction().

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The new check runs in the bushy-join loop of join search, and its planning-time cost is not measured.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Are the three join.sql plan changes from the has_join_restriction() fix worse, equal or better than the current plans?
Why is a local exception in join_search_one_level() preferable to setting lateral_referencers for joinrels, which message #1 says is always NULL?
Which branches should receive the fix, given that the bug reproduces on 14 through master?
Does the patch fix the 5-way and 6-way variants from message #1, and does it add regression tests for them?
What is the planning-time cost of the new check on queries with many relations and many PlaceHolderVars?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the join search code in joinrels.c and how PlaceHolderVars and lateral references restrict join order. No such committer has posted in the two visible messages.
committability.liability: The owner signs for join-order behaviour on all supported branches if back-patched, including any plan change or new "failed to build any N-way joins" case, and for keeping the new exception in step with has_join_restriction().
committability.author_follow_up: The author reproduced the bug, compared three fixes and asked for thoughts in message #2, which suggests he will follow up.

priority.reason: The patch is 2.1 KB in one file and fixes an internal planner error on valid SQL that reaches back to 14. The failing query shape is rare and was found by a fuzzer, but the choice between the three fixes needs a reviewer who knows join search.

provisional_note: Without the code, the exact condition of the exception, its cost when the PlaceHolderVar list is long, and whether it admits extra pairs that change plans on stable branches could not be judged. The prose does not show whether a regression test is included.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: postgres_fdw: evaluate placeholdervars on remote server
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets postgres_fdw evaluate PlaceHolderVars on the remote server, so left, right and full joins that contain PHVs can be pushed down. It also changes how whole-row references are deparsed and builds on the deparser support for subqueries from the full-join pushdown work.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author said he was not satisfied with the patch and that it needed more work, and he did not rebase it for the September 2017 CommitFest after reminders. Robert Haas proposed marking patches like this Returned with Feedback when no rebase arrives before the CommitFest starts, and the author agreed and marked it so.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Frankly, I think things where there was a ping multiple weeks before
the CommitFest started and no rebase before it started should be
regarded as untimely submissions, and summarily marked Returned with
Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add a greedy join search algorithm to handle large join problems
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add GOO (Greedy Operator Ordering), a greedy join search that repeatedly joins the legal pair with the lowest estimated cost until one join remains. It is meant to replace GEQO for queries above geqo_threshold, with optional heuristics such as result size, and a combined mode that picks the cheaper of several greedy plans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The author posted v5 on the day the entry was withdrawn and listed further work, while plan quality on realistic workloads was still under evaluation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict"
Reverted commit(s): Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit f0f2c0c1aef95757c4e7f144d5577e2b0d814279.

The original problem that led to the use of pg_restrict was that MSVC
couldn't handle plain restrict, and defining it to something else
would conflict with its __declspec(restrict) that is used in system
header files.  In C11 mode, this is no longer a problem, as MSVC
handles plain restrict.  This led to the commit to replace pg_restrict
with restrict.  But this did not take C++ into account.  Standard C++
does not have restrict, so we defined it as something else (for
example, MSVC supports __restrict).  But this then again conflicts
with __declspec(restrict) in system header files.  So we have to
revert this attempt.  The comments are updated to clarify that the
reason for this is now C++ only.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel grouping sets
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add parallel execution of GROUPING SETS queries by splitting aggregation into partial and final stages, first by grouping on the union of all grouping columns in workers and doing the grouping-sets aggregation in the leader. The later version instead performs grouping-sets aggregation in workers, tags each partial tuple with a grouping set ID, and has the leader combine results per grouping set, with refactoring of nodeAgg.c (phase reorganisation, sorting inside the Agg node).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last patch version received no review and no longer applied to HEAD. A PGCon hallway-track discussion of the approach concluded that nodeAgg.c needs refactoring before it is complicated further, and after an off-list discussion with Melanie, who had picked up the patch, the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There was also considerable discussion in a (virtual) hallway-track session
during PGCon which reviewed the approach (for lack of a better description),
deeming that nodeAgg.c needs a refactoring before complicating it further.

precedents_retrieved.title: Restrict EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) for RLS and security_barrier views
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch forbids EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) for statements that use row-level security or security_barrier views, so ordinary users cannot see how many rows the policy or view condition filtered out. Only members of a predefined role, proposed as pg_read_all_stats, could still run it in those cases.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed noted that the issue is not a security bug and that row counts can also be seen through pg_stat_get_tuples_returned(), pg_class.reltuples and plain EXPLAIN estimates, so EXPLAIN should stay as it is. After a discussion on pgsql-security, the author marked the patch rejected. The reason was that a determined attacker who can run arbitrary SQL can subvert row-level security anyway, so the restriction makes performance analysis harder without a real security gain.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Therefore, restricting EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) will do more harm than good, since it will make analyzing query performance harder without a real security gain.

precedents_retrieved.title: Restrict pg_rewind to specified/needed directories
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, David Steele, Stephen Frost
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_rewind synchronize only a fixed list of directories (base, global, pg_wal, pg_xact and other WAL-related directories), so it no longer copies logs, replication slots or configuration files from the source. The list of files is fetched with one query per listed directory.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to an include list: a directory missing from it, such as one added by a new feature or an extension, can make a rewind silently corrupt. They asked pg_rewind to reuse the exclude list that base backups already use, by moving it to common code, and to add an option for more exclusions. The patch stayed in Waiting on Author, and Michael Paquier returned it with feedback and said he would work on the exclude-list approach himself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Forgetting something in the
exclusion list just makes the process less efficient while forgetting
something in the inclusion list may mean breakage.

precedents_retrieved.title: Restricting maximum keep segments by repslots
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GUC, max_slot_wal_keep_size, that limits how much WAL replication slots can keep, so checkpoints remove older segments and slots that fall behind lose required WAL. It also adds wal_status and remain columns to pg_replication_slots and a checkpoint warning that names the affected slots.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was closed because the author did not respond to the latest review comments for about two months. Open points were Alvaro Herrera's API objections to GetLsnAvailability() returning a string, the slot-list warning function and the GetOldestKeepSegment change, plus Jehan-Guillaume de Rorthais's questions on the wal_status states and repeated warnings. Early in the thread Michael Paquier objected to the whole idea as a wal_keep_segments-like setting, but the patch later reached Ready for Committer.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread has been waiting for input from the patch author,
Horiguchi-san, for a couple of months now, so I am switching it to
returned with feedback in the CF app.

precedents_retrieved.title: Consider parallel for LATERAL subqueries having LIMIT/OFFSET
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes set_rel_consider_parallel so that a lateral subquery with LIMIT/OFFSET may still be considered for parallel query, so a Gather can go above the whole nested loop. A later version allows this only when rel->lateral_relids is not empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author argued that each outer row gets its own execution of the limited subquery, but Tom Lane (seen only in quoted text) and Robert Haas were not convinced this is safe. Tom Lane noted that the patch took any lateral dependency as enough, even one that does not feed the limited subquery. Robert Haas said the real issue is where parameters are set and used, which the LATERAL keyword does not capture. The commitfest manager returned it because no further review was coming, and asked for a more rigorous correctness argument or simpler constraints.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The problem here isn't created by LATERAL, but by parameters.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support run-time partition pruning for hash join
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch prunes Append subnodes on the outer side of a hash join while the hash table is built: each inner row computes the partitions it can match, and Append skips the others. The design, ported from Greenplum's Partition Selector, builds PartitionPruneInfos in createplan.c, stores pruning results in executor parameters, and can intersect results across several join levels.
precedents_retrieved.objection: David Rowley was concerned that pruning runs for every row put into the hash table, may prune nothing, and has no worst-case overhead figures. The patch's costing therefore chose the pruning hash join only in very conservative cases. He suggested a different first step, parameterized scan paths on the partition key so that parameterized nested loops can use the existing run-time pruning. Richard Guo found this promising, the thread moved to that design, and no new hash join patch appears.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Maybe instead of inventing a very pessimistic part prune Hash Join, it might be better to make the above work without the LATERAL + OFFSET 0 by creating the parameterized paths Seq Scan paths.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the precedent list has no row about this idea. Message #1 points to an earlier "failed to build any N-way joins" fix and says this query still fails with it applied, so that fix does not cover this case. No earlier rejection reason applies here.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch is a planner bug fix in joinrels.c with no new syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql change or dump format. Queries that now fail with an internal error would plan, and the author reports no plan changes in the regression tests. Back-patch scope and the plan stability of existing queries on stable branches could not be checked without the code.

The patch changes only join search pruning in joinrels.c. It touches no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or exported struct, so it holds no persistent or cross-node state. One ABI point is open: a back-patch to 14 must not change exported planner function signatures or RelOptInfo layout, and the prose does not say whether it does.

The patch changes only bushy-join pruning in the planner's join search. It adds no privilege, role, function, view or setting, and exposes no new data. An unprivileged user can already send queries with many relations, so the extra pairs the patch admits are not a new denial-of-service path. The security angle finds no objection.

This is a narrow planner bug fix in one file. It adds no user-visible surface. If the PHV list is empty, the extra check should cost almost nothing on the common path. Only the duplicated-rule concern applies from this angle.

This is a planner bug fix for an internal error, so no existing feature, extension or idiom meets the need. Setting join_collapse_limit = 1 and from_collapse_limit = 1 avoids the error, but only by giving up join reordering, so it is a workaround. The patch extends the existing pruning check in join_search_one_level() and adds no second mechanism.

This is a bug fix for an internal planner error ("failed to build any 4-way joins") on valid SQL. The report includes a reproducer, a bisect to a 2018 commit, and failures on 14 through master. Demand for a fix to a plan-time ERROR on legal queries needs no further evidence. Design and cost questions belong to other angles.
